title: Why did William win the Battle of Hastings?

review.note: Original content written without uploaded Year 7 lessons. Check against your lessons; add lesson page references in the Teacher area.

learn.intro: In 1066 England had three different kings in one year. This topic follows how William, Duke of Normandy, ended the year wearing the crown — and asks you to decide why he won.

sections.title: 1. The succession crisis

blocks.p: Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066 without any children. In Anglo-Saxon England there was no fixed rule that the eldest son, or nearest relative, automatically became king. The dying king's wishes, family links, power and the support of the Witan (the council of leading nobles and churchmen) all mattered.
Four men had a claim to the throne:

ul: Harold Godwinson — Earl of Wessex, the richest and most powerful noble in England, and Edward's brother-in-law. English sources say Edward named Harold as his successor on his deathbed. The Witan supported him.

William, Duke of Normandy — Edward's cousin (once removed). Norman writers claimed Edward had promised him the throne years earlier, and that Harold had sworn an oath to support William while visiting Normandy around 1064.
Harald Hardrada — King of Norway and a famous warrior. His claim came from an earlier agreement between King Magnus of Norway and King Harthacnut of England.
Edgar Ætheling — Edward's great-nephew and the closest blood relative, but a teenager with no army or powerful supporters.

blocks.p: Harold was crowned on 6 January 1066, the day after Edward died. Speed mattered: it made Harold king before anyone else could act — but it also gave William a reason to say Harold had broken his oath.

evidence: Edward died 5 January 1066; Harold crowned 6 January 1066.
Norman sources describe Harold's oath to William (c.1064); the Bayeux Tapestry shows an oath scene.

sections.title: 2. The Viking invasion and Stamford Bridge

blocks.p: Harold expected William to invade from the south, so he kept an army waiting on the south coast through the summer of 1066. By early September food was running out and men were needed for the harvest, so the army was sent home.

Then the danger came from the north. Harald Hardrada landed in Yorkshire with a large fleet, joined by Tostig — Harold's own brother, who had been exiled in 1065. On 20 September they defeated the northern earls Edwin and Morcar at the Battle of Fulford, and York surrendered.

Harold marched north at great speed, covering around 185 miles in a few days. On 25 September he surprised the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge. Hardrada and Tostig were both killed. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that only a small part of the invading fleet was needed to carry the survivors home.
It was a crushing victory — but Harold's army had lost men and was exhausted, and it was about 250 miles from the south coast.

evidence: Fulford: 20 September 1066 — Edwin and Morcar defeated.
Stamford Bridge: 25 September 1066 — Hardrada and Tostig killed.
Harold's men marched roughly 185 miles north in a few days.

sections.title: 3. William prepares and lands

blocks.p: William spent the spring and summer of 1066 preparing. He gathered soldiers from Normandy and neighbouring lands such as Brittany and Flanders, had a large fleet built and planned to ship horses across the Channel for his knights.
He also gained support from Pope Alexander II, who sent a papal banner. This allowed William to present the invasion as a just cause, which helped persuade men to join him.

For weeks the wind blew the wrong way and William's fleet could not sail. When the wind changed, he crossed quickly. He landed at Pevensey on 28 September 1066 — three days after Stamford Bridge, while Harold was still in the north. The south coast was undefended.
William moved to Hastings, built a wooden fort and let his men raid the surrounding countryside. Sussex was Harold's own family land, so this put pressure on Harold to come and fight quickly.

evidence: William landed at Pevensey on 28 September 1066.
Pope Alexander II sent a papal banner.
William's army included Normans, Bretons and Flemish/French soldiers.

sections.title: 4. The battle: 14 October 1066

blocks.p: Harold hurried south, stopping in London to gather more men, and reached the Hastings area on 13 October. He did not wait for all the troops who might have joined him. The battle took place on 14 October on a ridge about seven miles from Hastings, where the town of Battle now stands.
The armies were probably roughly the same size — historians' estimates are usually somewhere between 5,000 and 8,000 men each, but nobody knows for certain.

ul: The English fought on foot at the top of the ridge in a shield wall. At its heart were the housecarls — professional, well-trained soldiers, many armed with long two-handed axes. With them stood the fyrd: part-time soldiers called up from the shires, often less well equipped.

The Normans had three types of soldier: archers, foot soldiers and mounted knights. William's army was split into three divisions: Bretons on the left, Normans in the centre and French and Flemish soldiers on the right.

blocks.p: The fighting lasted most of the day. Early attacks uphill failed against the shield wall. When the Bretons fell back, some English soldiers broke ranks to chase them down the hill and were cut off and killed. A rumour spread that William was dead; according to Norman accounts he lifted his helmet so his men could see him — the Bayeux Tapestry shows this moment.

Norman writers say William then used feigned retreats: pretending to flee to draw more English soldiers out of the shield wall. Historians still debate whether these were deliberately planned or exaggerated later.
Late in the day Harold was killed, along with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine. Without their leaders, the English line broke.

evidence: Battle of Hastings: 14 October 1066, lasted most of the day.
Harold's brothers Gyrth and Leofwine were also killed.
The Bayeux Tapestry shows William lifting his helmet to show he was alive.

sections.title: 5. Explaining William's victory

blocks.p: Historians group the reasons for William's victory into factors. Your job is not just to list them but to show how they link together and decide which mattered most.

ul: William's leadership and preparation — a well-organised invasion force, ships, horses, papal support, and calm leadership during the battle (showing his face when rumours spread).
Norman army and tactics — a mix of archers, infantry and cavalry that could attack in different ways; possibly feigned retreats.
Harold's decisions — fighting quickly instead of waiting for more troops; possibly reacting to the raids on his lands.
English weaknesses — tired troops after Stamford Bridge; parts of the fyrd breaking the shield wall to chase the enemy.
Luck — the wind delaying William until Harold was in the north; Hardrada invading first; Harold being killed at a key moment.

blocks.p: Factors interact. For example, Hardrada's invasion was luck for William, but it only helped because Harold then rushed back south (a decision) with exhausted men (a weakness).

evidence: Three-day gap: Stamford Bridge (25 Sept) and William's landing (28 Sept).
English broke ranks to chase retreating Bretons.
Harold's death late in the day ended English resistance.

sections.title: 6. How do we know? The sources

blocks.p: Almost everything we know about 1066 comes from a small number of sources, most written by or for the winners. Always ask: who made it, when, and why?

evidence: The Bayeux Tapestry was probably made in the 1070s, likely for Bishop Odo, William's half-brother.
William of Poitiers was William's chaplain.

blocks.p: Victory at Hastings did not immediately make William king. In London the Witan chose Edgar Ætheling. William marched around London, burning land as he went, until the English leaders — including Edgar — submitted to him at Berkhamsted.
William was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day, 25 December 1066. It took years more fighting before the Normans fully controlled England.

vocab.def: Who takes over as ruler next.
A person who says they have the right to something — here, the throne.
The council of leading nobles and churchmen who advised the king and helped choose a new one.
A powerful Anglo-Saxon noble who governed a large region.
A professional, full-time soldier serving the king or an earl.
Part-time soldiers called up from the local area in times of war.
A line of soldiers standing close with overlapping shields to block attacks.
Soldiers who fight on horseback — the Norman knights.
Pretending to run away to trick the enemy into chasing and breaking formation.

misconceptions.wrong: The battle was fought in the town of Hastings.
misconceptions.right: It was fought on a ridge about seven miles away, where the town of Battle now stands.

misconceptions.wrong: Harold definitely died from an arrow in the eye.
misconceptions.right: The Bayeux Tapestry is ambiguous and may have been altered by later repairs; one early account describes Harold being cut down by knights. We cannot be certain.

misconceptions.wrong: The English army was just untrained peasants.
misconceptions.right: The housecarls were highly trained professional soldiers. The fyrd was part-time, but many were experienced.
The battle lasted most of the day and could have gone either way.

misconceptions.wrong: William became king as soon as the battle ended.
misconceptions.right: The Witan chose Edgar Ætheling first; William was crowned on 25 December after the English leaders submitted.
Normandy was a duchy whose rulers descended from Viking settlers. The duke owed loyalty to the French king but acted largely independently.

sources.title: The Bayeux Tapestry
sources.origin: Probably commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William's half-brother; likely embroidered in England.
sources.purpose: To tell the Norman story of 1066 and justify William's conquest — it emphasises Harold's oath.
sources.usefulness: Detailed images of weapons, ships and armour. Shows the Norman point of view; some scenes were restored centuries later.

sources.title: William of Poitiers, 'The Deeds of William' (Gesta Guillelmi)
sources.origin: Written by William's own chaplain, a Norman who had once been a soldier. He was not at the battle.
sources.purpose: To praise William and show his claim was rightful.
sources.usefulness: The fullest early account of the battle, including the feigned retreats — but strongly pro-William.

sources.title: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
sources.date: Entries written during and after 1066; several versions
sources.origin: Kept by English monks in different monasteries.
sources.purpose: To record important events each year.
sources.usefulness: An English point of view; brief on the battle itself; different versions sometimes disagree.

sources.title: The Song of the Battle of Hastings (Carmen de Hastingae Proelio)
sources.date: Possibly c.1067 — the date and author are debated
sources.origin: Often linked to Guy, Bishop of Amiens.
sources.purpose: To celebrate William's victory in verse.
sources.usefulness: Possibly the earliest account; gives a different description of Harold's death. Poetic and uncertain in date.

mcq.q: When did Edward the Confessor die?
mcq.why: Edward died on 5 January 1066; Harold was crowned the next day.

options: A council of leading nobles and churchmen
mcq.why: The Witan advised the king and backed Harold as Edward's successor.

mcq.q: Which claimant was Edward's closest blood relative?
mcq.why: Edgar was Edward's great-nephew, but he was a teenager without an army or powerful backers.

mcq.q: What did Norman writers claim Harold did in Normandy around 1064?
options: Swore an oath to support William
mcq.why: The oath gave William a reason to call Harold an oath-breaker — useful propaganda.

mcq.q: What happened at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066?
mcq.why: Harold surprised the Norwegians; Hardrada and Tostig were killed.

mcq.q: Where did William land on 28 September 1066?
mcq.why: Pevensey, on the Sussex coast — three days after Stamford Bridge.

mcq.q: Why was the papal banner useful to William?
options: It showed the Church backed his cause, helping recruitment
It was a signal for his ships
mcq.why: Church support made the invasion look just and encouraged men to join.
Housecarls were full-time, well-trained soldiers — often with two-handed axes.

mcq.q: Where did the English army stand at the start of the battle?
mcq.why: Harold's shield wall held the high ground, forcing the Normans to attack uphill.

options: Pretending to flee to draw the enemy out
mcq.why: Norman writers say this pulled English soldiers out of the shield wall. Historians debate how far it was planned.

mcq.q: Why did William lift his helmet during the battle?
options: To show his men he was alive
mcq.why: A rumour of his death was spreading panic; showing his face steadied his army.

mcq.q: Which is the best example of LUCK helping William?
options: The wind delaying him until Harold went north
mcq.why: The timing was outside William's control and left the south coast undefended.

mcq.q: Who probably commissioned the Bayeux Tapestry?
mcq.why: Odo was William's half-brother — so the Tapestry shows the Norman point of view.

evidence.q: Give a precise piece of evidence that Harold's army was tired by October 1066.
evidence.model: They had fought at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, after marching about 185 miles north in a few days, then marched back south — about 250 miles — to face William.

evidence.q: Give a piece of evidence that William prepared carefully.
evidence.model: He built a large fleet that could carry horses, gathered soldiers from Normandy, Brittany and Flanders, and won a papal banner from Pope Alexander II.

evidence.q: Give evidence that the shield wall was effective at first.
evidence.model: Early Norman attacks uphill failed against it, and the battle lasted most of the day.

evidence.q: Give evidence that luck helped William.
evidence.model: The wind kept William in Normandy until Harold was in the north fighting Hardrada; he landed unopposed on 28 September, three days after Stamford Bridge.

flashcards.a: Supplies were running out and men were needed for the harvest.

flashcards.a: Harold's exiled brother, who joined Hardrada's invasion.

flashcards.q: What happened at Fulford (20 Sept 1066)?

flashcards.q: What happened at Stamford Bridge (25 Sept 1066)?
flashcards.a: Harold surprised and defeated the Norwegians; Hardrada and Tostig were killed.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: Describe two claims to the English throne in 1066.
questions.asks: Give accurate details about two different claimants and what their claim was based on. You do not need to explain who was most likely to win.
steps: Pick the two claimants you know best.
For each: name them, say who they were, and say what their claim rested on.
Add one precise detail for each (a date, a person, an event).
questions.plan: 1 minute planning: write two names and one detail beside each. 6 minutes writing. 1 minute checking names and dates.
success: The basis of each claim stated accurately
At least one precise supporting detail for each
mistakes: Describing the battle instead of the claims
Writing about four claimants briefly instead of two in detail
Mixing up Harold Godwinson and Harald Hardrada

model.t: One claim was Harold Godwinson's. He was Earl of Wessex, the most powerful noble in England, and English sources say Edward named him as successor on his deathbed in January 1066.
model.n: Names the claimant, says who he was, gives the basis of the claim with a precise date.

model.t: The Witan, the council of leading nobles and churchmen, supported him, and he was crowned on 6 January.
model.n: Extra precise detail that strengthens the description.

model.t: A second claim was William of Normandy's. Norman writers said Edward had promised him the throne, and that Harold had sworn an oath to support William while in Normandy around 1064.
model.n: A different claimant; two parts to the claim; notes these come from Norman sources.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: Explain why the Battle of Stamford Bridge was important for the outcome of the Battle of Hastings.
questions.asks: Show how events in the north led to consequences in the south. Each paragraph needs a reason, evidence and an explanation of how it affected Hastings.
steps: Identify two or three effects of Stamford Bridge (e.g. tiredness, losses, the south left undefended).
Explain how that effect changed what happened at Hastings.
Finish by linking the effects together.
questions.plan: 2 minutes: list effects and evidence in the planning grid. 9 minutes: two PEEJ paragraphs. 1 minute: check every paragraph links back to Hastings.
success: Identifies at least two consequences of Stamford Bridge
Explains clearly how each affected Hastings
Shows a link between the consequences
mistakes: Telling the story of Stamford Bridge without linking it to Hastings
Saying 'the army was tired' without evidence
Forgetting dates that prove the timing

model.t: Stamford Bridge was important because it left the south coast undefended when William arrived.
Harold was in the north defeating Hardrada on 25 September, and William landed at Pevensey on 28 September, just three days later.
model.n: EVIDENCE — two precise dates show the timing.

model.t: This meant William could land his army and horses safely and choose where to wait, instead of fighting on the beach while his men were still unloading.
model.n: EXPLAIN — shows the consequence for William.

model.t: So Stamford Bridge gave William a strong start before the battle even began.
model.n: JUDGEMENT/LINK — ties the paragraph back to the outcome at Hastings.

full: POINT: One reason Stamford Bridge mattered was …
JUDGEMENT: Therefore this helped William win at Hastings by …

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question (central enquiry)
questions.q: 'William won the Battle of Hastings mainly because of luck.' How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Weigh luck against other factors (William's leadership, Norman tactics, Harold's decisions, English weaknesses) and reach a clear judgement about which mattered most.
steps: Decide your judgement before you write — agree, partly agree or disagree.
Paragraph on luck, with evidence and explanation.
Paragraphs on one or two other factors.
Compare: which factor mattered most and why? Use the judgement questions.
Conclusion that answers 'how far' and explains your reasoning.
questions.plan: 4 minutes planning grid (factor / evidence / how it helped William / how decisive). 18 minutes writing. 3 minutes conclusion and check.
success: Clear judgement in the introduction and conclusion
At least one other factor explained with precise evidence
Factors compared directly, not just listed
Conclusion gives a reason for the judgement
mistakes: A conclusion that sits on the fence with no reason
judgementPrompts: How long did this factor matter for? (duration)
How much of the battle and campaign did it affect? (scope)
How directly did it lead to the victory? (effectiveness)
What would have happened without it? (impact)

model.t: I partly agree: luck gave William important chances, but his leadership was what turned those chances into victory.
model.n: Introduction states a clear, balanced judgement.

model.t: Luck helped William because the wind delayed his crossing until Harold was fighting Hardrada in the north. He landed unopposed at Pevensey on 28 September, three days after Stamford Bridge.
However, luck alone did not win the battle. When rumours spread that he had died, William lifted his helmet to show he was alive, stopping a panic that could have ended the battle.
Leadership mattered more because it affected the whole day, whereas the lucky timing only decided where and when the battle started.
model.n: Direct comparison using scope and duration.

stretch.task: Draw a chain of at least four links from 'Edward dies without children' to 'Harold is killed at Hastings'. For each arrow, write how one event caused the next.
Rank the five factors from most to least important. Then move your top factor to the bottom and write the strongest argument you can for why it really belongs there. Has your view changed?
Historians debate whether the feigned retreats were a deliberate tactic or a story told later by Norman writers. Using what you know about who wrote the sources, explain why we cannot be sure.
If the wind had changed in August and William had landed while Harold's army was still waiting on the south coast, who would have won? Use evidence about the two armies to justify your prediction.

The Bayeux Tapestry and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle tell different stories about 1066. Using their origin and purpose, explain why they might disagree and which you would trust more for each of: Harold's oath; the course of the battle.
After Hastings, the Witan still chose Edgar Ætheling. What does this tell us about how much changed on 14 October, and how much stayed the same until Christmas?
